entry.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
entry.summary: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

entry.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
entry.summary: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

entry.title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
entry.summary: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.

entry.title: A Geometric Calderón Problem for Differential Forms
entry.summary: We establish boundary determination and global partial-data uniqueness for Karpukhin's Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator on differential $p$-forms. We derive an explicit recursion for its full symbol and determine the full boundary jet of the metric, modulo conformal gauge in the critical dimension $n=2p+2$. For $p\geq1$, partial data determine metrics that are analytic in the interior and near the measured boundary subset, up to isometry or conformal equivalence. The global uniqueness relies on a new projection-kernel embedding that detects the unobserved boundary through rank loss and small eigenvalues. We also establish global partial-data uniqueness for smooth metrics with harmonic curvature, using elliptic-transport unique continuation and, in the critical dimension, conformal-geodesic coordinates. A Weyl nondegeneracy condition further upgrades conformal equivalence to isometry.

entry.title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
entry.summary: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

entry.title: Toward high-throughput, low-latency structural biology using light, Part I: Protein-ligand pose determination
entry.summary: We demonstrate for the first time that an optical spectroscopy - electron-vibration-vibration two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (EVV 2DIR) - has sufficient structural competence to enable the reconstruction of the three-dimensional geometries of drug-protein binding at the level needed for practical drug discovery applications. Klug et al. previously demonstrated experimental detection of drug binding to a kinase using EVV 2DIR. Here we use a quantum mechanical approach to calculate and assign elements of EVV 2DIR spectra for the spectral region 1200-1800 cm$^{-1}$ / 1100-1800 cm$^{-1}$ of 92 protein-ligand complexes. This dataset includes ligand-target poses drawn from existing crystal structures and ligand-target poses created by docking and cofolding models. We find that binding-dependent spectral features are robust, interpretable, and consistent across poses in a given binding mode, and distinct for each unique hydrogen bonding geometry. We construct a spectral distance metric to distinguish poses that conform to the ligand-target hydrogen-bonding pattern of the crystal structure from those that do not. These results show that, given a set of predicted ligand-target poses containing the correct geometry, the hydrogen-bonding pattern of the valid pose may be rapidly identified by comparing simulated and experimental EVV 2DIR spectra. Finally, we discuss the practical implications for a new, high throughput structural biology for drug discovery that will be the subject of forthcoming manuscripts, noting that the base technologies to perform EVV 2DIR quickly and efficiently already exist and will enable a novel structure to be determined in only minutes for each sample. Moreover, this can be achieved without the need for crystallization, isotopic labeling, or low temperatures, non-destructively using picogram quantities of material.

entry.title: Efficient search for microlensed gravitational-wave signals with matched filtering and a two-image statistic
entry.summary: Gravitational waves from compact binary coalescences can be microlensed by compact objects along the line of sight, producing frequency-dependent waveform distortions. As standard matched-filter searches rely on unlensed templates without accounting for lensing effects, microlensed signals can lose signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) through template mismatch and suffer further losses from signal-consistency tests. We quantify both effects for the $\texttt{PyCBC}$ search using microlensed injections in simulated data. The two losses occupy different regions of lens parameter space in the geometric optics representation: template mismatch is governed by the relative magnification of the two images, while the consistency-test penalty is governed by their time delay. We show that a microlensed signal lies in the two-dimensional subspace spanned by a template and its time-shifted copy, allowing the relative magnification and Morse phase to be maximized over analytically, leaving only the time delay to search. The resulting statistic requires no extension of the template bank and reduces the median loss in re-weighted SNR from $10\%$ to $1.6\%$, and the $90^\mathrm{th}$ percentile from $41\%$ to $9\%$. At a false-alarm rate of one per day, the relative detection volume improves by about $6\%$ across all injections, and by a factor of $1.9$ for the $10\%$ of injections most affected by lensing. In addition to increased detection capacities, we also show how the detection statistic can be used to establish the lensed nature of the trigger. Therefore, the work proposed here lays the foundation for an effective search and identification of microlensed signals in gravitational-wave data.

entry.title: AMISS: An Integrity Framework for Magnetic Navigation
entry.summary: Magnetic Navigation (MagNav) is a promising alternative to traditional systems like Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), offering resistance to jamming or spoofing attacks to which the latter are vulnerable. MagNav matches scalar magnetic measurements over time against a known map of Earth's magnetic anomaly in order to position a vehicle. MagNav is therefore sensitive to the quality of these maps, especially to errors in the survey data that the maps are derived from. In order to be a reliable and mature navigation technology, MagNav must satisfy integrity requirements for mitigation of such faults. To this end, a solution-separation monitoring algorithm is developed that performs a role equivalent to Advanced Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (ARAIM) in GNSS, which detects faults as well as generates worst-case bounds (protection levels) on estimation error for faults too small to be detected. It is shown how these integrity methods can be developed in a \emph{windowed-in-time} sense, where subsets of measurements over a time window are compared with each other in order to detect outliers that can potentially result from errors in the map. The applicability of the approach is demonstrated using results obtained using synthetic aircraft data with injected faults.

entry.title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
entry.summary: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

entry.title: CREST: A Hardware-Aware GNN-Based Framework for High-Fidelity and Robust Superconducting Quantum Compilation
entry.summary: Quantum compilation on superconducting processors requires selecting a connected execution region whose topology and calibrated properties suit the input circuit. This choice constrains subsequent routing and influences the noise encountered during execution, yet aggregate hardware-quality metrics alone may not reliably predict the execution fidelity of a given circuit. Calibration updates can also change region suitability and trigger the rebuilding of calibration-dependent resource structures. We present CREST, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework that evaluates circuit-region compatibility before routing. It encodes gate dependencies and logical-qubit interactions alongside each candidate region's connectivity and current calibration attributes; bidirectional cross-graph attention relates the two representations, while real-device execution outcomes supervise candidate ranking. The trained scorer is reused with updated calibration attributes. Evaluations on 324 circuits from seven datasets on TianYan-176 show that CREST improves mean measurement-distribution fidelity by 19.03% over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest mean fidelity on every dataset. Furthermore, using updated calibration attributes, the same trained model maintains the highest overall mean fidelity across six measurement dates without retraining. With a unified model of circuit-region compatibility, CREST improves execution fidelity across diverse workloads and sustains that advantage as hardware calibration changes.

entry.title: Quantum Simulation of First-Quantised Chemistry with a Sum-of-Squares Representation
entry.summary: Calculating molecular energies is expected to be an important application of quantum computers, but the most efficient algorithms to achieve this typically have significant space requirements. Scaling quantum processors to thousands of logical qubits is a daunting engineering challenge, so developing algorithms that run with reduced qubit requirements is of particular importance. Moreover, most algorithms are benchmarked on active spaces with about as many orbitals as electrons, missing dynamical correlation which is necessary to describe real chemistry. Capturing this correlation requires several times more orbitals than electrons, even in compact atomic-orbital basis sets. This low-filling regime favours first quantisation, where each electron is represented by a number of qubits that grows only logarithmically with the number of orbitals. Whether this approach translates into a practical advantage in orbital basis sets of realistic size, however, has been unclear. Here, we develop a first-quantised phase estimation algorithm for generic orbital basis sets, based on a non-convex sum-of-squares representation of the Hamiltonian and spectral-gap amplification. We compare it with the state-of-the-art second-quantised algorithm, compiling both with the same techniques at the logical level. For six molecules with 4 to 24 electrons in 5 to 14 times as many orbitals, our first-quantised method needs up to 16 times fewer Toffoli gates than the second-quantised algorithm in the low-qubit regime, where only a few hundred logical qubits are available. It stays cheaper up to between several hundred and about 1\,400 qubits, and its smallest qubit count is 1.4 to 2 times lower than in second quantisation. In the low-qubit and low-filling regime, our algorithm is therefore the method of choice for chemistry in orbital basis sets.

entry.title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
entry.summary: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

entry.title: Communications-free Collective Intelligence Via Allocentric Belief
entry.summary: A team of skilled card players share no information amongst each other, and yet still are able to coordinate their play by watching the same players and reading the same tells. Autonomous systems have failed to exploit this logic, relying instead on explicit communication or complex state estimation schemes that can fail when it matters most. Without it, decentralized agents diverge in their world beliefs, and coordination collapses. Here we show that anchoring all agents to a single shared external actor, a common witness whose reactions encode team state, produces spontaneous, communication-free coordination. An allocentric belief network trained on witness behavior allows each agent to independently reconstruct full team state, keeping group beliefs consistent with no inter-agent exchange. Across five competitive environments allocentric belief alignment outperforms egocentric approaches in collective performance, and even scales to sixty-agent teams where standard methods fail. These results establish a new principle for collective intelligence: in the absence of communication, a shared gaze replaces a shared channel.

entry.title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
entry.summary: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

entry.title: Potential spectral markers of intrinsic magnetic fields of hot exoplanets in the UV range
entry.summary: A method for detecting the intrinsic magnetic fields of exoplanets, based on the effect of atomic alignment (the redistribution of populations among magnetic sublevels under the action of anisotropic radiation from the host star), has been adapted for observations with the Spektr-UV space telescope. A procedure for selecting sensitive transitions is proposed, and triplet absorption lines in the UV range that are sensitive to alignment are identified. On the basis of three-dimensional aeronomic models of the hot Jupiters KELT-20 b and HAT-P-32 b, absorption spectra in these lines are calculated for cases with and without intrinsic magnetic fields of the exoplanets. Using the Spektr-UV exposure-time calculator, the observability of the effect is assessed, and an observing program is proposed, specifying the optimal duration of individual exposures and the number of transits required to detect the signal.
